scientificSummary.scope: Bounded primary (autoantibody-mediated) membranous nephropathy map: podocyte target antigens (PLA2R1, THSD7A and other recently described antigens) lumped as one shared antigen-antibody mechanism, subepithelial immune-complex formation, complement activation, podocyte injury and nephrotic proteinuria. Secondary membranous nephropathy (lupus, malignancy, infection, drug-associated) and therapy efficacy are excluded.

paragraphs.text: Primary membranous nephropathy shares an antigen-specific podocyte autoantibody principle, but antigen-defined subtypes differ in frequency, serology and clinical associations and are increasingly treated as partly distinct entities. Autoantibodies, IgG4-predominant though not IgG4-exclusive, bind a podocyte-associated antigen, not all of which are cell-surface proteins: PLA2R in most inspected adult cases, THSD7A in a smaller PLA2R-negative subgroup, NELL-1 in a further share of PLA2R-negative cases that varies widely by cohort, and semaphorin 3B, HTRA1 or rarer putative targets beyond those. The evidence differs in kind by antigen: deposit-eluted IgG recognized PLA2R and THSD7A, patient sera recognized NELL-1, semaphorin 3B and HTRA1, and the seven putative mass-spectrometry targets were recovered from immune complexes and co-localized with IgG in the deposits without comparable serological evidence. Anti-PLA2R levels tracked clinical status and proteinuria, and epitope spreading beyond the cysteine-rich domain was an independent risk factor for poor renal outcome. HLA-DQA1 and PLA2R1 risk loci were associated with biopsy-proven disease in white-ancestry cohorts.

Antigen-specific rodent models supply the directional evidence: podocyte expression of human PLA2R1 produced antibodies, subepithelial deposits and nephrotic syndrome, lymphocyte-deficient animals developed neither, and Thsd7a-knockout mice were protected from antibody transfer. These do not show that every human subtype shares one effector route. Complement is consistently involved but heterogeneously so. All three initiation pathways were present in patient biopsies with proximity assays favouring the classical pathway, yet factor-B-null mice were protected and lectin-pathway blockade preserved synaptopodin and NEPH1 in podocyte culture; no initiating route is established as universal in humans. Effector evidence conflicts directly: C5b-9 assembly was required for slit-protein proteolysis in culture and C5 deficiency partly reduced albuminuria, while membrane-attack-complex inhibition left albumin permselectivity unchanged on a glomerulus-on-a-chip and anti-THSD7A antibodies injured podocytes in C3-deficient mice. The under-1-to-4.9% frequencies apply only to the seven putative targets, not to NELL-1, which was more often malignancy-associated than other antigen types, so part of NELL-1 disease falls outside this primary-only scope. That scope is a curation choice, not a claim that the primary-secondary split is current practice; claims rest on agent-inspected abstracts, no therapy is curated, and appraisals are uncalibrated.

after.text: In a small retrospective antigen-subtype comparison, NELL1-associated membranous nephropathy showed lower glomerular C3 and C4d deposition than PLA2R-associated disease. This qualifies extrapolation of a uniform complement-injury pathway across antigen subtypes; deposition differences do not directly establish functional complement activity or slit-diaphragm injury.
limitations: Small retrospective cohort with antigen-associated differences in age and chronic damage; residual confounding remains.
C3, C5 and factor H proteomic differences were numerically higher in PLA2R-associated MN but not statistically significant.
C4d did not significantly correlate with serum anti-PLA2R titres. C4d deposition alone does not identify classical versus lectin pathway activity.
The study did not directly test complement-mediated slit-diaphragm damage; the finding is a scope qualification to that branch, not a new causal experiment.
